opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing I've learned from Jensen is how he thinks about time horizons. Most companies plan around the next quarter or the next product cycle. Jensen tends to ask a different question: if this technology really works, what will the world look like in ten years, and are we willing to start building for that world today, even when the market doesn't exist yet?

CUDA is the classic example. When NVIDIA started investing in general-purpose GPU computing, there wasn't an obvious business case. It cost a lot, it hurt margins for years, and many people outside the company didn't understand why a graphics company was doing it. But Jensen believed that accelerated computing was a fundamental shift, so he stayed with it for more than a decade. When deep learning arrived, the platform was already there. That kind of patience is rare.

For me as a researcher, this has changed how I choose problems. Early in my career, I was more focused on what could produce a strong paper in the next six months. Working at NVIDIA, I started asking whether a direction would still matter in five or ten years. That's part of why I've spent so much time on generative models and, more recently, world models and physical AI. When we started working on things like image synthesis, some people saw it as a fun demo. But we believed that if machines can generate and simulate the visual world, that becomes a foundation for robotics, autonomous driving, and many other physical applications. Projects like Cosmos come from that long-term bet.

Another thing I've learned is that long-term doesn't mean slow. Jensen is very patient about the direction, but very impatient about execution. He wants you to move fast, ship, learn, and iterate, while keeping the north star fixed. So I try to hold both ideas together: be stubborn about the vision, be flexible about the path.

He also talks about reasoning from first principles instead of following what everyone else is doing. If you only follow the crowd, you're always late. So when my team considers a new direction, we try to ask: what is fundamentally true about this problem, and what will be inevitable eventually? If we believe something is inevitable, then the question is simply whether we want to be the ones who build it. Usually, the answer is yes.

r001.rationale: The response says Jensen reasons from first principles rather than following the crowd, asking what is fundamentally true and inevitable when considering a direction.

r002.rationale: Liu says Jensen’s approach changed how he chooses problems: he shifted from near-term paper results toward work that could matter in five or ten years.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest thing I learned from Jensen is that he doesn't make decisions based on what the market is telling him today. He makes them based on where he believes the technology is going, and then he's willing to wait a very long time for the market to catch up.

CUDA is the obvious example. For years, people asked why NVIDIA was spending so much on a software platform that didn't seem to generate revenue. He kept investing anyway, because he believed accelerated computing would eventually matter. When deep learning arrived, everything was already in place.

I joined NVIDIA Research in 2016, and I saw the same pattern up close. Jensen would support research directions that had no clear product tied to them, as long as he believed the underlying problem was important. Generative models were like that for a while. We were working on image synthesis, video synthesis, simulation, and at the time a lot of it looked like interesting demos with no obvious business. He never asked us to stop. He asked us what it would take to make it work.

What that taught me is to separate two questions. The first is whether something is going to be important. The second is when it's going to be important. Most people conflate them, and they give up on things that are clearly important just because the timing is uncertain. Jensen is very comfortable being early. He accepts that being early looks like being wrong for a long time.

The other thing I absorbed is his idea of "zero billion dollar markets." He'd rather build for a market that doesn't exist yet than fight over one that already does. That shaped how I think about my own work. When we started on world models and physical AI, there was no customer asking for it. But if you believe robots and autonomous systems need to understand the physical world, then someone has to build the foundation, and it's better to be the one who started five years before it became obvious.

So practically, when I evaluate a research bet now, I ask: if this works, does it change what's possible? If the answer is yes, I don't worry too much about whether it pays off next quarter. That patience is something I got directly from watching him.

r001.rationale: The response says Jensen bases decisions on where he believes technology is going rather than current market signals, and supports bets based on underlying problems he considers important.

r002.rationale: Ming-Yu says watching Jensen taught him to separate importance from timing and shaped how he evaluates his own research bets, including not focusing on next-quarter returns.

astra-6.text:
What I’ve learned from Jensen is to start with a view of the future and reason backward: if we believe something will become important, what do we need to build today to be ready for it? That’s a different way of thinking from asking what will produce an immediate return.

In research, that perspective matters because the most promising ideas often take time to prove themselves. You need conviction to keep investing before the results are obvious, but you also need to keep learning and testing your assumptions. For me, the influence is to think beyond the next paper or the next milestone—to ask whether we’re building a capability that could matter over many years.

r001.rationale: The response describes reasoning backward from a view of the future and looking beyond immediate returns, but does not say to choose a direction based on underlying fundamentals rather than outside signals.

r002.rationale: The candidate says Jensen’s approach influenced him to think beyond the next paper or milestone and consider capabilities that could matter over many years.

sol-6.1.text:
What has influenced me most is the willingness to commit to a long-term direction even when the immediate return isn’t obvious. In research, it’s easy to focus on the next paper or the next benchmark. But some important ideas need sustained investment before you can really see their value.

The way I think about that is to be patient with the ambition, but rigorous about the progress. You keep asking whether you’re learning, whether the technical foundations are getting stronger, and whether your assumptions still hold. Long-term conviction doesn’t mean ignoring evidence. It means giving a promising direction enough time and resources to develop while continuing to challenge your thinking.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses committing to a long-term direction and checking progress, but does not describe a first-principles rule based on fundamentals rather than outside signals.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the influence was committing to a long-term direction and applies that approach to their own research decisions.
